q: Salento's leading red carries a name usually read as black and bitter. Name the grape.
exp: The everyday reading is black and bitter, though philologists more often trace it to the Latin niger and the Greek mavros, both simply meaning black. It makes deep reds and some of Italy's best-regarded roses.

q: Basilicata's DOCG rank applies only to a longer-aged version of its one famous red. Which word marks that on the label?
exp: The standard bottling remains a DOC and only the extended-ageing wine was promoted. Volcanic soils and altitude on the Vulture give the acidity that carries the wine through those years.

q: A sweet passito made in a town at the southern tip of Calabria carries the town's name. Name the wine.
exp: The grapes are dried on mats in the sun on a stretch of coast facing Sicily. The wine is amber, orange-scented and made in tiny quantity, and the town really is called Bianco.

q: Etna's vineyards are mapped by contrada. What does that term denote?
opts: A named district of the mountain
A style of low bush training
A cooperative cellar shared by growers
exp: The contrade are administrative parcels strung along the northern, eastern and southern flanks, the DOC leaving the west out, and growers now use them much as Burgundy uses climats, so many appear on labels. Soil, altitude and lava flow age change sharply between neighbouring ones.

q: One Marsala grade forbids the sweetening additions the others permit. Which grade is it?
exp: Vergine takes no cooked must and no mistella, so it is dry and shaped entirely by long oxidative ageing. The other grades may be adjusted for colour and sweetness.

q: Grillo arose as a crossing of which two Sicilian grapes?
exp: The Muscat parent explains the faint grapey lift in a grape otherwise known for body and resistance to oxidation. Those qualities are why it became the backbone of good Marsala.

q: Etna Bianco Superiore may be grown in one commune only, on the eastern flank. Name it.
exp: Milo faces the Ionian sea and catches most of the rain that reaches the mountain, which suits Carricante's late ripening. The Superiore rules also demand a higher share of that grape.

q: Nerello Mascalese must lead an Etna Rosso, with a softer partner permitted alongside. Name that partner.
exp: Cappuccio brings colour and flesh where Mascalese brings perfume, tannin and acidity. Its name describes the cloak of leaves the vine throws over itself.

q: Sweet passito from the Aeolian islands north of Sicily is named for the largest island of the group. Name the wine.
exp: Salina rather than Lipari itself grows most of it, on volcanic terraces above the sea. The grapes are dried on racks and the wine comes out amber, apricot-scented and lightly herbal.

q: Which Sicilian white is the island's most planted variety, long used as base wine for Marsala?
exp: It crops generously and was for decades sent north or distilled rather than bottled with any ambition. Lower yields and earlier picking have shown it can make a serious dry white.

q: Ungrafted bush vines more than a century old grow in deep sand in Sardinia's southwest. Which denomination covers them?
exp: The sand of Sant'Antioco and the Sulcis coast defeated phylloxera, so old own-rooted alberello vines survive. The wine is fuller and riper than Carignan usually manages in France.

q: A Sardinian white ages under a film of yeast in part-filled casks in the Tirso valley. Which wine is it?
exp: The flor works as it does in Jerez, and the wine emerges dry, nutty and high in alcohol without being fortified. It has nothing to do with Vernaccia di San Gimignano in Tuscany.

q: Vermentino reaches its most concentrated form on the island in a northeastern zone of decomposed granite. Name that zone.
exp: Granite sand drains fiercely and holds the vines short of water, which concentrates the fruit. The rest of the island bottles the grape under a broader denomination covering all of Sardinia.

q: Sardinia's Spanish centuries left a Catalan-speaking town in the northwest whose name marks a DOC. Name the town.
exp: Aragon repopulated the town from Catalonia in the fourteenth century and the language held. The DOC is unusually permissive, covering a long list of varieties in every colour.

q: A white variety brought over from Spain survives almost nowhere but around Alghero. Name it.
exp: It nearly disappeared and was kept going by a single large producer in the town. The wine is dry, saline and firmer than most Mediterranean whites of its weight.

q: Which red grape gives Sardinia a light everyday DOC bottled under its own varietal name across much of the island?
exp: Monica makes a soft, low-tannin red for drinking young, quite unlike Cannonau in weight. It is planted widely enough to carry an island-wide denomination of its own.
